name: Reykjavik
tagline: A small northern capital between volcano, ocean and aurora.
whenBlurb: June to August brings the midnight sun and open roads; September to April, dark skies for the northern lights. Choose your light and dress for weather.

ourTake.lede: Reykjavik is really a warm, walkable base camp, you come for what's a short drive out, not for the city itself, though its restaurants and pools are genuinely good. Skip the Blue Lagoon near the airport for the quieter Sky Lagoon or a rural geothermal pool, and treat the town's public baths as the real local ritual. For the northern lights, base here in winter but be willing to chase clear skies with a private guide rather than trust a coach tour.
ourTake.comeIf: You want raw landscape, glaciers, geysers, and hot springs, used as a base for the Ring Road.
ourTake.skipIf: You want warmth, beaches, or Indian food on tap; this is cold, costly, and elemental.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: The Retreat at Blue Lagoon
items.description: Iceland's standout luxury address, a 60-suite hotel carved into an 800-year-old lava field, with its own private geothermal lagoon and a subterranean spa.

items.name: The Reykjavik EDITION
credentials: Home to Tides, MICHELIN Guide restaurant (2026)
items.description: The city's most polished international flagship, Ian Schrager's EDITION on the harbourfront beside the Harpa concert hall, with mid-century Nordic design by Roman and Williams.

items.name: Hotel Borg
items.description: Reykjavik's original grande dame, an elegant 1930 Art Deco house on the parliament square, and long the first address for visiting dignitaries.

items.name: Iceland Parliament Hotel, Curio Collection by Hilton
items.description: Hilton's most upscale Reykjavik house, a set of historically protected old-town buildings beside the Alþingi parliament, with a serious spa and wellness floor.

items.name: Sand Hotel
items.description: One of the most stylish stays in the capital, a design-led boutique on the main shopping street, next to the century-old Sandholt bakery whose breakfast it borrows.

items.name: Hallgrímskirkja & the Tower
items.description: Reykjavík's great expressionist church rises like a basalt-column cliff over the whole city, a 74-metre concrete spire visible from almost everywhere. Take the lift up the tower for the clearest 360-degree view of the coloured rooftops, the bay and the mountains beyond; on a clear day you can see the Snæfellsjökull glacier across the water. Go at opening or near closing for quiet, and time a stop for the vast Klais pipe organ.

items.name: Harpa Concert Hall
items.description: A honeycomb of coloured glass on the harbour's edge, designed with artist Ólafur Elíasson, the light through its facets shifts all day and glows at night. Even without a concert it is worth wandering the free public levels for the geometry and the sea views; for a special evening, book the Iceland Symphony Orchestra or a private tour. An easy, warm indoor anchor for a multi-generational group in bad weather.

items.name: Sun Voyager (Sólfar) Sculpture
items.description: Jón Gunnar Árnason's steel dreamboat sits on the seafront pointing north across the bay to Mount Esja, not a Viking ship but an ode to the undiscovered, best at sunset or under the midnight sun when the light runs gold along the water. A short, photogenic stroll from Harpa; pair it with a walk along the Sæbraut path.

items.name: The Old Harbour (Grandi)
items.description: The working harbour turned into the city's most characterful quarter, this is where whale-watching and puffin boats leave, and where the old fish sheds now hold the Marshall House galleries, the Whales of Iceland exhibition and some of the best cooking in town. A relaxed half-day of galleries, ice-cream at Valdís and a warm bowl of lobster soup, with the boats coming and going.

items.name: Laugavegur & Skólavörðustígur Shopping
items.description: The main artery of downtown and its rainbow-painted side street climbing to Hallgrímskirkja, the place for Icelandic design, 66°North and Farmers Market outerwear, hand-knitted lopapeysa sweaters, and boutiques of local jewellery and ceramics. Compact and walkable; a fine afternoon for the family with cafés and bakeries every few doors. Fine dining is here too, though strictly vegetarian tables are limited, book ahead and flag dietary needs.

items.name: Perlan, Wonders of Iceland
credentials: World's first indoor ice cave built from real snow
items.description: A glass dome set atop the city's hot-water tanks, now Iceland's best natural-history experience: walk through a real indoor ice cave carved from 350 tonnes of mountain snow, feel a simulated glacier and volcanoes, and lie back for the 8K Áróra planetarium show that explains and recreates the Northern Lights, a guaranteed aurora even in summer or cloud. The wraparound observation deck gives a full-city panorama. Genuinely engaging for children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Sky Lagoon
items.description: The most design-led of the city's geothermal baths, an infinity edge that dissolves into the North Atlantic, so you soak in steaming water while the horizon and the sunset fill your view. The seven-step Skjól ritual (warm lagoon, cold plunge, sauna, mist, scrub, steam, shower) is a spa in itself. Book the Sér package for private changing rooms; a discreet, grown-up alternative to the Blue Lagoon and only minutes from downtown.

items.name: Laugardalslaug Geothermal Pool
items.description: The everyday heart of Icelandic life, the largest public geothermal pool in Reykjavík, with an Olympic pool, hot pots at different temperatures, a steam bath and water slides. This is where locals actually gather; the ritual is simple and cheap and deeply restorative after a cold day. Bring the whole family, remember the local etiquette of a thorough shower before entering.

items.name: The National Museum of Iceland
items.description: The clearest window into the country's story, from the ninth-century settlement and the Vikings through a thousand years to independence, told through swords, carved church doors, silver and dress. Compact, well-lit and calm; a private guide brings the sagas alive for teenagers and gives a grandparent the through-line before the landscape does the rest.

items.name: Reykjavík Art Museum, Hafnarhús
items.description: The main downtown site of the city's art museum, in a converted harbour warehouse, best known for its permanent room of Erró, the Icelandic pop-collage master, alongside bold contemporary shows. Three sites share one ticket (Hafnarhús, Kjarvalsstaðir and the Ásmundarsafn sculpture house), a good rainy-day trio for an art-minded family.

items.name: Tjörnin (The Pond) & City Hall
items.description: The little lake at the city's heart, ringed by pastel timber houses and alive with more than forty species of bird, the reason it is nicknamed 'the biggest bread soup in the world' for the children who come to feed the ducks and swans. City Hall on its shore holds a huge 3-D relief map of Iceland worth a look. A gentle, pretty loop for grandparents and small children.

items.name: Grótta Lighthouse & Seltjarnarnes
items.description: At the city's edge, a lighthouse on a tidal islet reachable on foot at low tide, with a warm little geothermal foot-bath (Kvika) beside the path. Because it faces away from the city lights it is Reykjavík's best in-town spot for the Northern Lights in winter and for the midnight sun in summer. A quiet, wild-feeling walk minutes from downtown, check the tide before crossing.

items.name: Whale Watching from the Old Harbour
items.description: Boats leave straight from downtown into Faxaflói Bay to find minke and humpback whales, white-beaked dolphins and porpoises, roughly a three-hour trip with a high success rate from April to October. For a family, charter a private RIB or a larger stable vessel; wrap up warm, as the wind on the water is the cold you feel most in Iceland.

items.name: Puffin Watching to Akurey & Lundey
items.description: In summer, short boat trips run from the Old Harbour to the low islands of Akurey and Lundey, home to tens of thousands of nesting puffins, the comical, orange-billed sea-parrots that are Iceland's most-loved bird. A gentle hour on the water, ideal for children; often combined with a whale trip. Strictly a summer sighting, the puffins leave by mid-August.

items.name: Whales of Iceland Exhibition
items.description: A hangar of 23 life-size whale models, including a full 25-metre blue whale, suspended overhead so you grasp the true scale of the animals you hope to see at sea. A warm, indoor complement to a boat trip and a hit with younger children on a wet afternoon.

items.name: The Blue Lagoon
items.description: Iceland's most famous experience, milky-blue, silica-rich geothermal water steaming against black lava, with a swim-up bar, silica masks and the luxurious Retreat Spa and hotel for those who want privacy. It sits between the airport and the city, so it makes a perfect first or last stop. Note honestly: it is close to the Reykjanes volcanic zone and has occasionally closed at short notice for air-quality or seismic reasons, confirm status the day before and let your advisor keep watch.

items.name: The Golden Circle, Þingvellir National Park
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Þingvellir National Park
items.description: The first and greatest stop on the classic day loop, a rift valley where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates visibly pull apart, and where Iceland's Vikings founded the world's oldest surviving parliament, the Alþingi, in 930 AD. Walk the Almannagjá gorge literally between two continents; the certified can snorkel the glass-clear Silfra fissure. A private guide turns the geology and the history into one story for the whole family.

items.name: The Golden Circle, Geysir Geothermal Area
items.description: The steaming valley that gave the world the word 'geyser'. The original Geysir is now mostly dormant, but its neighbour Strokkur erupts a column of boiling water eight to ten metres high every few minutes, reliable, thrilling and safe from behind the ropes. Mud pots and hot springs bubble all around; a natural, easy wonder for children and grandparents.

items.name: The Golden Circle, Gullfoss Waterfall
items.description: The 'Golden Falls', a glacial river thundering in two great tiers into a rugged canyon, often crowned with a rainbow in the spray. It was saved from a hydro dam a century ago by a farmer's daughter who threatened to throw herself in, and remains one of Iceland's most powerful sights. Viewing platforms suit every mobility level; go with a private super-jeep to reach it before the coaches.

items.name: The South Coast, Seljalandsfoss
items.description: A slender 60-metre waterfall that pours over a former sea cliff, and the rare one you can walk behind, into the mist-filled hollow, for a view out through the falling water. Bring waterproofs; the path gets slick. Nearby, the hidden Gljúfrabúi falls tucks inside a mossy canyon for those willing to wade a few steps. A dramatic first stop on any South Coast day.

items.name: The South Coast, Skógafoss
items.description: A perfect 60-metre-wide curtain of water crashing off the old coastline, so broad and consistent that it throws double rainbows on sunny days. Climb the staircase to a viewing platform at the lip, or simply stand at the base and feel the roar. A superb picnic and photo stop; legend says a Viking's chest of gold lies hidden behind the falls.

items.name: The South Coast, Reynisfjara Black-Sand Beach
items.description: A shore of jet-black volcanic sand backed by a cathedral of hexagonal basalt columns, sea caves and the Reynisdrangar sea stacks rising offshore. Otherworldly and beautiful, but the 'sneaker waves' here are genuinely dangerous and have killed the unwary; never turn your back on the sea and keep children well up the beach. A guide who knows the safe line makes all the difference.

items.name: Vík í Mýrdal
items.description: Iceland's southernmost village, a red-roofed church on a green hill above black beaches and sea stacks, the natural lunch-and-refuel point on a South Coast day and the gateway to the wider Katla region. Small, scenic and welcoming; a good place for a warm bowl of soup before the drive back or on toward Jökulsárlón.

items.name: Sólheimajökull Glacier
items.description: The most accessible glacier tongue from the capital, a river of blue-and-ash ice you can walk right up to, and, with a certified guide, crampon onto for a glacier hike or ice-climb. It is a moving, sobering sight: markers show how far the ice has retreated in a decade. Always go with a licensed guide; the crevasses are lethal to the unprepared. A once-in-a-lifetime walk for able members of the family.

items.name: Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Vatnajökull National Park
items.description: Iceland's crown jewel, a deep lagoon where a glacier tongue calves electric-blue and black-streaked icebergs that drift slowly to the sea, with seals basking among them. A zodiac or amphibious-boat cruise weaves you between the bergs. It is a long drive best done as an overnight or by private aircraft for a day; sitting within Vatnajökull National Park, it is worth every hour.

items.name: Diamond Beach
credentials: Part of Vatnajökull National Park, UNESCO World Heritage Site
items.description: Just across the road from Jökulsárlón, the icebergs that reach the sea wash back onto black volcanic sand as glittering, translucent chunks, 'diamonds' scattered on jet velvet, catching the low sun. Utterly photogenic and constantly changing with the tide; pair it with the glacier lagoon on the same visit.

items.name: Northern Lights (seasonal, Sep–Apr)
items.description: The aurora borealis, green and violet curtains rippling across the winter sky, is the reason many come to Iceland. You need dark, clear skies away from the city, so a private guide chases the forecast to the best spot, or you watch from a countryside lodge or a glass-roofed cabin. Never guaranteed on a single night, so give it several; a warm flask, a tripod and patience are the tools. Grótta and Þingvellir are strong, close options.

items.name: The Reykjanes Peninsula & Volcanic Zone
items.description: The dramatic lava peninsula between the airport and the city, geothermal fields at Gunnuhver and Seltún, the Bridge Between Continents spanning the mid-Atlantic rift, and the Fagradalsfjall lava fields born of the 2021–2023 eruptions, which certified guides now lead hikes across. Note honestly: this is Iceland's most active zone, the newest eruption sites near Grindavík stay closed for safety, and access shifts with conditions, go only with a licensed local guide who tracks the daily reports.

items.name: The Snæfellsnes Peninsula
items.description: Called 'Iceland in miniature', one peninsula holding a glacier-capped volcano (the Snæfellsjökull of Jules Verne's Journey to the Centre of the Earth), black-pebble beaches, lava fields, fishing villages and the endlessly photographed Kirkjufell mountain with its waterfall. A superb full-day private tour with fewer crowds than the Golden Circle; the light and the emptiness feel like the real Iceland.

items.name: Kirkjufell & Kirkjufellsfoss
items.description: The 'church mountain', a perfect arrowhead peak beside a tiered little waterfall, one of the most photographed scenes in Iceland and a Game of Thrones filming location. Best at sunset or under the aurora. A quick, rewarding stop on a Snæfellsnes day for anyone with a camera.

items.name: Silfra Fissure Snorkelling
credentials: Within Þingvellir, UNESCO World Heritage Site
items.description: Drift between two continents in the clearest natural water on earth, glacial meltwater filtered through lava for decades, with visibility beyond 100 metres, held at a steady near-freezing chill inside a warm drysuit. No diving certificate is needed for the snorkel; it is a bucket-list first for confident swimmers among the family. Book well ahead and go with a licensed operator only.

items.name: Ice Caves & Glacier Hikes (seasonal, Nov–Mar)
credentials: Within Vatnajökull National Park, UNESCO World Heritage Site
items.description: In winter, guides lead you into the naturally-formed blue ice caves beneath the Vatnajökull ice cap, glowing, cathedral-like chambers that melt and re-form each year, and onto the glacier tongues in crampons. This is genuine once-in-a-lifetime terrain, but strictly seasonal and only ever safe with a certified glacier guide; the caves and crevasses are deadly to the unguided. Best combined with a Jökulsárlón overnight.

items.name: Reykjadalur 'Hot River' Valley Hike
items.description: A steaming valley an hour's hike into the hills above Hveragerði, where a natural geothermal river runs warm enough to bathe in, you soak in the open air with the moss and mountains around you. About a 3-km walk each way; a lovely, active, free alternative to the built lagoons for those who like to earn their soak.

items.name: The Kerið Volcanic Crater
items.description: A 3,000-year-old crater with steep red-and-black caldera walls cradling a startling aquamarine lake, a small, easy, beautiful stop often added to the Golden Circle. A short rim walk gives grandparents the view; the fitter can descend to the water's edge.

items.name: Fontana Geothermal Baths & Rye-Bread Baking
items.description: Lakeside geothermal pools and steam rooms built over natural hot springs on the Golden Circle route, where the staff dig warm dark rye bread out of the black sand it bakes in overnight. A relaxed, low-key soak with a lake to plunge into, a gentler, more local counterpoint to the Blue Lagoon, easy to fold into a Golden Circle day.

items.name: The Settlement Exhibition (Reykjavík 871±2)
items.description: Built around the excavated ruins of one of the oldest houses in Iceland, a genuine Viking-age longhouse dated to around 871 AD, displayed in situ under the modern city with clever projections that rebuild the hall around you. A compact, atmospheric half-hour that grounds the whole trip in where Reykjavík began.

items.name: Árbær Open Air Museum
items.description: An old turf farm turned into a village of relocated historic houses, timber and turf-roofed homes furnished as they were, with staff in period dress, a smithy and old cars. It shows how Icelanders actually lived across the last centuries; a charming, gentle outing for grandparents and children when the weather turns.

items.name: Videy Island
items.area: Off the Old Harbour / Skarfabakki (short ferry)
items.description: A car-free island a short ferry from the city, with birdlife, walking paths, a 1755 stone church and Yoko Ono's Imagine Peace Tower, a column of light beamed into the sky each winter in memory of John Lennon. A peaceful half-day away from the streets, and one of the best quiet spots near the city for the aurora.

items.name: Mount Esja Hike
items.description: The flat-topped mountain that fills Reykjavík's northern skyline and changes colour through the day, a well-marked, popular hike straight from a car park at its base, with turning points to suit any fitness. The Þverfellshorn viewpoint rewards you with the whole city and bay spread below. A satisfying half-day for the active in the family.

items.name: Kjarvalsstaðir, Reykjavík Art Museum
items.description: The light-filled modernist pavilion of the city art museum, in a leafy park, devoted largely to Jóhannes Kjarval, the beloved painter who taught Icelanders to see their own lava and moss as landscape. Quieter than the harbour site and shares the same three-in-one ticket; a calm hour with a café and a park for the children outside.

items.name: Café & Bakarí Culture, Sandholt and Braud & Co
items.description: Icelandic bakery culture is a genuine pleasure, Sandholt's pastries on Laugavegur and the graffiti-fronted Brauð & Co are institutions, alongside the famous kleinur and cinnamon buns. A warm, welcoming refuge between sights, and reliably good for a vegetarian traveller, for whom Reykjavík's dedicated veg-friendly spots (like Gló) are easiest found downtown.

items.name: Icelandic Phallological Museum
items.description: Reykjavík's most famously quirky museum, the world's only collection devoted entirely to phallic specimens from Icelandic mammals, presented with genuine scientific earnestness and a wink. A only-in-Iceland curiosity and a talking point for adult travellers; best appreciated by grown-ups.

items.name: Hljómskálagarður Park & the Sculpture Trail
items.description: The green lung on the south shore of the Pond, dotted with statues and framed by the little bandstand that gives it its name, a soft, unhurried place to walk off a big meal, let children run and see the city breathe. Loveliest in the long summer evenings.

items.name: Helicopter Flight over Volcano & Glacier Country
items.description: The most discreet and dramatic way to grasp Iceland's scale, a private helicopter lifting straight from the city to land on a glacier, circle the Reykjanes lava fields, or crest a crater rim, all in a couple of hours. It turns a full-day drive into a morning and gives elderly or time-short members of the family the wonders without the road. The definitive splurge for a multi-generational trip.

items.name: Dill
items.description: Iceland's most celebrated restaurant and the first in the country to win a star, Gunnar Karl Gíslason's New Nordic cooking, shaped by landscape, season and scarcity, through fermentation, smoking and curing.

items.name: Óx
items.description: Iceland's most intimate starred experience, a hidden 17-seat counter (set within Sümac) where chef Þráinn Freyr Vigfússon hosts a multi-course dinner that feels closer to a private kitchen gathering than a restaurant.

items.name: Moss
items.area: Grindavík / The Retreat at Blue Lagoon (nearby)
items.description: The starred table at The Retreat, seasonal tasting menus drawn from Iceland's mountains, rivers and seas, served on the edge of the Blue Lagoon lava field.

items.name: Tides
items.description: The Reykjavik EDITION's restaurant, an elegant, harbourfront room celebrating Icelandic produce and the sea, from the hands of a team with real pedigree.

items.name: Brút
items.description: Clean, elegant seafood cooking in one of the oldest buildings in Reykjavik, fish and shellfish handled with minimal intervention, letting the central ingredient shine.

items.name: Sümac
items.description: A lively modern brasserie with an exposed charcoal grill, Icelandic ingredients given a Middle Eastern and North African turn, from Lebanese to Moroccan.

items.name: Matur og Drykkur
items.description: 'Food and drink' in Icelandic, lovingly researched traditional Icelandic cooking, drawn from old cookbooks and thoughtfully updated for today.

items.name: OTO
items.description: An assured Italian–Japanese crossover, think lobster cappelletti with yuzu kosho, bringing a lighter, more international register to the city's dining.

items.name: Skúli Craft Bar
credentials: Reykjavik's leading craft-beer bar (Guide to Iceland; Vogue Scandinavia)
items.description: The city's temple to Icelandic craft beer, 14 rotating taps and well over a hundred bottles, in a cosy wood-panelled room named for a founding father of Reykjavik.

items.name: Kaldi Bar
credentials: Iceland's pioneering microbrewery bar (CNN Travel; Culture Trip)
items.description: The downtown bar of Iceland's first microbrewery, Czech-method beers brewed with northern spring water, plus the city's largest gin selection, in a warm, locals-heavy room.

items.name: Apótek
credentials: Widely listed among Reykjavik's best bars (Guide to Iceland; Culture Trip)
items.description: A handsome lobby bar in a grand former pharmacy on the old-town corner, prescription-themed cocktails mixed by resident 'pharmacists' in one of the city's most elegant rooms.

items.name: Loftið
credentials: Featured in CNN Travel and Vogue Scandinavia bar guides
items.description: An upstairs, vintage-glamour cocktail lounge with worn leather sofas and big windows over the walking street, the city's most grown-up drinking room.

plan.heading: 3 days in Reykjavik, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Hallgrímskirkja and its tower for the coloured rooftops, then the old harbour and Harpa concert hall.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The National Museum of Iceland, then coffee and pastries at Sandholt on Laugavegur.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Dill, the country's first Michelin star, tasting the New Nordic larder near the water.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Thingvellir at the continental rift with a private guide, before the coaches reach Geysir.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Gullfoss in full flow, then the tomato greenhouse lunch at Friðheimar on the way back.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An evening at the Sky Lagoon's private wing, then a light dinner at ÓX if a seat is held.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A helicopter or private drive to the black sands at Reynisfjara and the Seljalandsfoss falls.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch on the coast, then the Blue Lagoon's Retreat spa on the way to the airport.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A final dinner at Sumac in Reykjavik if the return allows, otherwise an early flight.

items.name: 101 Reykjavik (city centre)
items.description: The walkable heart around Laugavegur and Hallgrímskirkja, best for first-timers who want restaurants and bars on foot.

items.name: Old Harbour (Grandi)
items.description: Reclaimed warehouses now full of galleries and cafés, and where whale- and puffin-watching boats depart.

items.name: Laugardalur
items.description: Greener and calmer, built around the city's big geothermal pool, good for families and a more residential stay.

events.name: Iceland Airwaves
events.note: The country's landmark music festival, with gigs in venues and record shops across downtown Reykjavik.

events.name: Reykjavik Culture Night (Menningarnótt)
events.note: A single night when the whole city opens its doors with concerts, art and a harbour fireworks finale.

events.name: Winter Lights Festival
events.note: Museums, pools and buildings lit up across the darkest weeks, paired well with aurora season.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay centrally near the harbour or Laugavegur; weather is the true master here, so keep plans flexible for aurora and glacier days, dress in serious layers year-round, and book any private guide or helicopter well in advance as capacity is limited.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: You land at Keflavík Airport (KEF), about 45 minutes by private car to Reykjavík, with a chauffeur meeting you and, if you wish, routing you via the Blue Lagoon on the way in.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: The town itself is walkable but Iceland's draw is beyond it, so a private driver or a chartered vehicle is essential for the glaciers, waterfalls and the interior; a helicopter is the discreet way to the remoter sights.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is excellent in and around the capital and along the ring road; an eSIM works well, though signal thins in the remote highlands.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Icelandic króna; the country is almost entirely cashless, so cards and contactless cover everything, and tipping is genuinely not expected.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: June-August brings the midnight sun, mild days and open Ring Road, best for landscapes; the aurora is impossible then. September-March is dark enough for northern lights, with November-February coldest and stormiest.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No non-stop from India; cleanest routing is via London on British Airways or via Helsinki on Finnair (about 14h total), also via Frankfurt on Lufthansa/Icelandair. Premium cabins run only to the European hub, so the transatlantic-style leg to Keflavik is short-haul; book the hub lounge for the layover.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required; Iceland's tap water is among the world's purest and cold water is glacial-clean. One of the safest countries anywhere; the real risks are weather, wind and driving on remote roads, so use guided transfers in winter.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian choice is limited but growing; Indian food exists. Gandhi and Indian Curry House cover Indian and vegetarian needs; Jain is hard locally, so plan ahead and expect to self-cater on longer country trips.
